# My grooming van almost caught fire. Here’s what I should have checked before trusting the build.

At about 2:15 on Wednesday, October 28, I was standing in a client’s driveway in Bedford with Moose, a very large Bernese Mountain Dog, and my dryer on high.

Then I smelled hot plastic.

My first thought was that the dryer motor was overheating. Dryers make weird smells sometimes, especially when they’re full of dog hair, so it wasn’t an immediate red alert in my brain. Then I saw smoke coming from the bench seat where my batteries are.

That was the moment everything changed very quickly.

I killed the battery switch, got Moose out through the side door while he was still damp, and used the extinguisher briefly. Honestly, I’m still not sure whether I needed to or whether everything had already stopped when I cut the power. I wasn’t exactly taking notes at the time.

When I looked afterwards, the lug on the positive battery-to-inverter cable was black. The cable jacket had melted back about three centimetres.

Everyone is okay. Moose was actually pretty thrilled about the whole thing, because from his perspective the dryer stopped and then he got to have an unexpected driveway adventure. I was less thrilled. Moose’s mum brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook, which I will never forget.

I’m writing this because my whole income depends on that van, because I’m going to be off the road for weeks, and because Tasha is literally about to pay a deposit to the same person who built mine.

Tasha, please read this before you do.

And to be completely clear: **I’m a dog groomer, not an electrician.** Everything technical below comes from my own equipment labels, my photos, and what Priya from Sackville Marine Electric showed and explained to me afterwards. This is not a guide to rewiring your van. If anything sounds familiar, get a qualified person with high-current DC experience to inspect your setup.

## The setup I had

For reference, my van was built by Coastline Van Fitouts, owned by Darren, in spring 2025.

The electrical equipment I had was:

- A **3000W inverter**
- **Two 200Ah lithium batteries**
- A **12V system**
- A main battery-to-inverter cable marked **4 AWG**
- A **300A ANL fuse**, mounted roughly **90cm from the battery**
- The smoke detector in the cab that came with the van, but **no smoke detector in the rear grooming/electrical area**

It all looked neat. The bench was tidy, the wiring was tucked away, and nothing looked like a pile of spaghetti. I took that as evidence that the person building it knew what they were doing.

That was a mistake.

**Tidy is not the same thing as right.**

## What Priya found

There wasn’t one single thing that made me go, “Oh, that tiny part caused everything.” It was more like several decisions stacked on top of one another.

### 1. The main cable was too small for this installation

Priya told me that the 4 AWG battery-to-inverter cable was not appropriate for my 3000W inverter setup. Her assessment was that it should have been **2/0 cable** — that’s “two-aught,” not ordinary 2 AWG.

I want to phrase that carefully. I am not saying that every inverter installation everywhere can be judged using one simple chart, or that I now know how to size cable because somebody explained it to me once. Proper sizing depends on things like the continuous and surge current, the lowest battery voltage the system can operate at, the length of the cable run, voltage drop, insulation temperature rating, ambient temperature, how the cable is bundled or enclosed, and the manufacturer’s installation instructions.

But the basic problem with a mobile grooming van is that we can put serious, sustained loads on an inverter without thinking of ourselves as people running serious electrical equipment.

We just think, “I’m drying a dog.”

### 2. The positive lug had not been crimped properly

According to Priya, the lug on the positive end appeared to have been crushed with something like pliers or a hammer, rather than crimped with a proper tool matched to the lug and cable.

The heat-shrink was covering it.

I’m not saying the heat-shrink proves anyone deliberately concealed something. Heat-shrink is used over plenty of perfectly good connections. What I mean is that, from the outside, I had absolutely no way of seeing the quality of the crimp underneath.

Priya explained that a poor crimp can create a small area with higher electrical resistance. Instead of electricity passing cleanly through a solid, properly formed connection, that connection can start generating heat.

The important thing for me to understand was that **a cable does not have to be visibly undersized or melting along its whole length for a termination to become dangerous**. The damage can be concentrated at one lug. In my case, that was exactly where the blackening and melted jacket were.

### 3. The fuse position left too much cable unprotected

My 300A ANL fuse was installed approximately 90cm from the battery. Priya told me that, under the marine practices and standards she works from, main battery overcurrent protection would generally be within roughly **18cm, or about seven inches, of the source**, subject to the specific rules and exceptions.

Mine was nowhere near that.

The simple way I now understand it is this: the fuse needs to protect the cable coming from the battery. If there is a long stretch of cable before the fuse, a fault in that stretch does not have that fuse doing the job you probably assumed it was doing.

The exact distance and acceptable exceptions are things for a qualified installer to determine. I’m not suggesting everyone grab a tape measure and start relocating fuses themselves. That would be an extremely bad takeaway from this post.

The useful takeaway is to ask: **Where is the main fuse, how far is it from the battery measured along the actual cable route, and why is that acceptable for this system?**

### 4. A fuse does not protect you from a hot, badly made connection

This was the part that really made my brain stop.

I used to think of a fuse as the thing that would “trip” before anything got seriously out of hand. But a fuse responds to current. It is not sitting there measuring how warm a lug is getting.

A resistive, poorly crimped connection can overheat without drawing some dramatic spike beyond the fuse rating. The system can keep operating while the connection itself gets hotter and hotter.

So no, having a large fuse does not make a poor connection safe.

The fuse also has to be appropriate for the battery system, not just have a plausible number printed on it. Priya’s repair quote includes a **Class T fuse** and a new fuse block. She explained that lithium battery banks can deliver extremely high fault currents, so the fuse’s DC rating and interrupt rating matter. It has to be capable of safely interrupting the fault current the battery bank could potentially deliver.

That does **not** mean “ANL fuses are always bad” or “buy any Class T fuse and your van is fixed.” The complete device, ratings, cable, battery bank, holder, and installation have to be considered together. This is absolutely a professional-specification job.

### 5. There was no detector near the equipment that smoked

The only smoke detector was the one in the cab that came with the van. There wasn’t one in the rear area where I work and where the battery and inverter equipment lives.

A detector would not have corrected the crimp or resized the cable. It is prevention only in the sense that it might give you an earlier warning; it does not fix the electrical problem.

But I now think it’s worth asking a qualified installer what detection is appropriate for the rear grooming and electrical areas of a working van, particularly one that may have animals in it. I wouldn’t just stick any random household alarm beside a battery compartment and assume the location is correct. Vehicle vibration, temperature, airflow, equipment compartments, and manufacturer instructions all matter.

## The maths, in groomer language

I never understood how much current my equipment could pull because I only ever thought in watts. Watts are on the dryer. Amp-hours are on the batteries. That was more or less where my understanding ended.

Priya gave me a much more useful way to think about it.

For a simple DC estimate:

**Amps = watts ÷ volts**

But because the dryer is an AC load running through an inverter, you also have to account for inverter losses. A rough example using 90% efficiency is:

**Battery current = AC load watts ÷ (battery voltage × 0.90)**

Ninety percent is just an example for the maths, not a measurement of my inverter.

My dryer pulls approximately **1800–2000W** on high.

At exactly 12V, before accounting for inverter losses:

- 1800W ÷ 12V = **150A**
- 2000W ÷ 12V = about **167A**

Using that example efficiency of 90%:

- 1800W ÷ (12V × 0.90) = about **167A**
- 2000W ÷ (12V × 0.90) = about **185A**

That is for the dryer alone. The water heater sometimes runs as well, adding more load.

At full rated output, a 3000W inverter would draw approximately **250A at 12V before losses**. Using the same 90% example, that becomes roughly **278A**. If battery voltage drops while the inverter is still supplying the same output power, current can be higher again. Surge and startup requirements are separate considerations.

So when we talk about 150A, 185A, 250A, or more in a 12V grooming van, these are not absurd numbers invented to make the post sound dramatic. They follow directly from the kind of loads we use.

Also, having two 200Ah batteries does not magically make the main cable adequate. Amp-hours tell you something about stored capacity. They do not tell you the cable size is correct, the lugs are properly terminated, or the fuse system is suitable. You need the batteries’ continuous discharge specifications and battery management system limits too.

That was a lot for me to learn while looking at a melted cable.

## The thermal-camera comparison was the moment it really clicked

Priya showed me my damage photos alongside thermal-camera images from her own van running a similar kind of load.

Hers barely gets warm.

It wasn’t a laboratory-controlled comparison, and I’m not going to invent temperatures I didn’t record. But visually, the difference was wild. She could show me what properly selected and terminated equipment looked like under load, rather than simply telling me to trust her.

That is something I would now specifically ask for on a new build: **a commissioning test under a realistic load, including thermal inspection of accessible connections and components.**

Not just, “We switched it on and the dryer worked.”

Of course it worked. Mine worked too, right up until it didn’t.

## Tasha: get this in writing before you pay a deposit

Tasha, I am not asking you to take my word as an electrical expert. I’m asking you not to pay a deposit based only on photographs, verbal reassurance, or the fact that a previous van looked clean and professional.

Ask the builder for the design and specifications **in writing**, and ideally have someone independent review them. If a builder considers that unreasonable, that tells you something useful before your money is gone.

Here’s the list I would now use:

1. **Can I have a wiring diagram?**  
   It should show the batteries, inverter, chargers and charging sources, main disconnects, fuse blocks, and protective devices. Not just a sales drawing of where the cupboards go.

2. **What is the inverter’s continuous rating and surge rating?**  
   And what maximum DC current has the designer allowed for, including operation at lower battery voltage?

3. **What cable size is being used for each main run?**  
   Ask for the actual AWG or metric size, insulation/temperature specification, and approximate length. Include both positive and negative inverter runs. “Heavy-duty cable” is not a specification.

4. **Why is that cable size suitable?**  
   The answer should account for current, run length, voltage drop, installation conditions, and the inverter or battery manufacturer’s instructions.

5. **What are the battery bank’s continuous discharge limits?**  
   The amp-hour capacity alone is not enough. The builder should also know the BMS limitations and have specifications for the actual batteries being installed.

6. **What exact fuses or breakers are being installed?**  
   Ask for manufacturer, model, amp rating, DC voltage rating, and interrupt rating where applicable. A photograph of a fuse holder with a red cover is not enough.

7. **Where will the main battery protection be located?**  
   Ask for the intended distance from the battery terminals, measured along the cable run, and the standard or manufacturer instruction being followed.

8. **How will the lugs be terminated?**  
   Ask what lugs and crimping system will be used. I would now specifically ask whether main lugs will be crimped using a properly matched tool, not improvised with a hammer or pliers.

9. **Will the completed system be load-tested?**  
   Ask what load, for how long, and whether accessible cables, lugs, fuse holders, and the inverter area will be checked with a thermal camera.

10. **What smoke detection and fire equipment are included?**  
    Ask about the rear workspace and electrical area, not just whatever the base vehicle already has.

11. **Will an independent electrical inspection be allowed?**  
    I would want the right to have the design and finished work checked by a qualified person who does not work for the builder.

12. **What exactly is covered by the workmanship warranty, and for how long?**  
    “I stand behind my work” is not the same as a written warranty and a person who answers after something goes wrong.

For the record, as of writing this, Darren has not answered three texts and an email from me. I’m not going to invent a reason for that. I’m also not claiming to know what is inside anyone else’s van. This post is about what was found in mine, and I’ll update it if I hear back.

## A checklist you can use on your own van — with the power off

This is a **visual, information-gathering checklist**, not an electrical inspection and not permission to start pulling your system apart.

Before opening any accessible electrical area, follow the equipment manufacturer’s shutdown procedure. Switch off appliances and the inverter, address shore power, solar, alternator charging or other energy sources as applicable, and isolate the battery system as instructed. If you do not know how to do that safely, stop there.

A battery disconnect switch may not make every conductor safe. Lithium batteries themselves remain energetic. Do not loosen terminals, remove fuses, peel back heat-shrink, or disconnect battery leads as part of this checklist. Take photographs and call a professional if you find something concerning.

### Check the paperwork

- Do you have a wiring diagram?
- Can you identify the inverter’s continuous and surge ratings?
- Do you know the battery voltage, capacity, and continuous discharge specification?
- Do you have make and model information for the main fuse or breaker?
- Do you have the actual installation manual, rather than only a sales brochure?

If the answer to all of these is no, that is your first job: get the information from the builder or equipment labels.

### Read what is printed on the cable

Without pulling anything apart, see whether the accessible main battery-to-inverter cable has a visible size marking, such as 4 AWG, 2/0 AWG, or a metric size.

Photograph the marking and record the approximate length of the run. If it is unmarked, ask the builder or your inspector how its size and specification can be verified.

Do not use a random internet chart to declare it safe. Take the actual numbers to a qualified person.

### Look along every accessible section

With everything shut down and without bending or moving the cable, look for:

- Melted, bubbled, brittle, or shrunken insulation
- Brown or black discolouration
- Any sign that insulation has pulled back from a lug
- Cuts, rubbing, crushing, or chafing
- Cable pressing against sharp metal
- Missing grommets where cable passes through metal
- Cable resting against something that gets hot
- Corrosion or exposed, damaged strands at visible terminations
- Cable weight hanging from a lug instead of being properly supported

Conduit and cable loom can protect against abrasion, but they can also hide damage. A neat wrap is not an inspection result.

### Look at the visible lugs — but don’t dismantle them

If you can see a termination without disassembling anything, look for corrosion, cracked insulation nearby, unusual discolouration, or strands that appear damaged or poorly captured.

Do not tug on the lug to “test” it. Do not retorque a terminal because you watched somebody do it online. Lug type, crimping, terminal torque, and access all matter.

If heat-shrink or a cover prevents you from seeing the crimp, that does not mean it is bad. It means you cannot assess it visually. Ask a professional how it should be inspected.

### Photograph the fuse and record its position

Read and photograph everything printed on the main fuse or breaker and its holder.

Record:

- Amp rating
- Type, such as ANL or Class T
- DC voltage rating
- Manufacturer and model, if visible
- Its approximate distance from the battery along the cable path

Never install a bigger fuse because an existing one blows. Never replace one type with another solely because a blog says it sounds safer. Have the complete protection system specified and checked.

### Check whether you actually know how to shut everything down

Could you safely stop the inverter and isolate the battery in a hurry? Are there other charging inputs that still leave equipment energised? Is anything blocked by grooming equipment, dog crates, towels, or storage?

Knowing where a switch is does not help much if you have never read what it does.

### Check your warning and emergency equipment

- Do you have suitable detection in the rear work/electrical area as well as the cab?
- When was the detector last tested according to its instructions?
- Is your extinguisher accessible, inspected, and appropriate for the risks in your vehicle?
- Do you actually know how to use it?
- Can you get yourself and a dog out quickly without climbing past the electrical compartment?

For the van-specific answer on detector and extinguisher selection and placement, ask a qualified installer or fire-safety professional.

### Get an infrared thermometer, but don’t let it give you false confidence

After this, I bought a cheap infrared thermometer for **C$40 at Canadian Tire**. I think every groomer should have one.

But it is a screening tool, not a certificate of safety.

A basic infrared thermometer measures surface temperature. It does not see inside a crimp, and readings from shiny metal can be misleading. Do not open live covers or put your hands near terminals to get a reading. Please do not deliberately load up a suspect system to see how hot you can make it.

The safer approach is to have a professional establish and inspect a baseline under normal working conditions. If your system has been checked and is considered safe to operate, an infrared thermometer can still help you notice a change on an accessible exterior surface, such as the outside of equipment or a cable jacket.

The useful warning is not some universal magic temperature printed in a blog. It is **unexplained heat, a change from normal, one connection getting much hotter than a comparable one, or heat accompanied by smell, damage, or discolouration**.

If that happens, stop using the system and have it inspected.

## If you smell hot plastic or see smoke

Do not finish the dog first. Do not turn the dryer off and keep working because the smell fades. Do not open the bench and start touching things.

Stop the load and isolate power only if you can do so safely without moving towards smoke or exposing yourself to a live or damaged system. Get yourself, the dog, and other people away from the van. Call emergency services for smoke or fire. An extinguisher is for a small, manageable situation when you know how to use it and have a clear escape — not a reason to delay getting out.

And afterwards, don’t simply replace the visibly melted bit and go back to work. The reason it melted matters.

## Where I’m at now

The repair quote is **C$4,200**. It includes rewiring the main runs, installing a new fuse block and Class T fuse, and correcting the system rather than just replacing the damaged lug. The current estimate is **at least three weeks**, with parts on order.

I have cancelled **31 appointments so far**. Insurance has said “maybe,” which is apparently a category of answer you can receive while your entire business is sitting still. The adjuster is due on Thursday.

Rent is due on the first. I’m scared, and I’m not going to pretend this is just an interesting technical lesson now. That van is my income. It is how I get to every single dog I groom. I keep thinking about how ordinary the moment was: driveway, dryer, damp dog, appointment schedule running through my head.

I trusted the build because it looked tidy. I didn’t ask for cable sizes. I didn’t ask where the fuse was mounted. I didn’t know what a proper crimp looked like, and I would not have known what to look for underneath the heat-shrink anyway.

Customers should not have to become electricians before hiring a van builder. But I do now think we need to ask much better questions, get the answers in writing, and pay for independent inspection when we can — especially when our grooming equipment puts sustained, high-power loads on a 12V system.

For now, Moose is fine, I’m fine, and I’m extremely grateful for a client with coffee and a front step. My van is not fine. I’m waiting on parts, the adjuster, and a proper repair, and Darren still has not responded as of this writing.

I’ll post another update when the van is back, including what was replaced and what I learn during the recommissioning. Until then, please don’t assume your system is safe just because it works, looks tidy, or has never given you a problem before.
